Welcome! I'm so glad you're here. My name is [Your Name], and I'm a clinician specializing in postpartum mental health. I'm here to support you during this significant time in your life. As part of our conversation today, I'll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS, to help us understand your emotional well-being during the postpartum period.

The EPDS is a validated tool that helps us identify any potential concerns related to depression and anxiety that some new mothers may experience. I'll be asking you 10 questions, and I want to reassure you that this is a safe and confidential space for you to share your feelings. Your responses will help me better understand your needs and provide the support that's right for you.

Before we begin, I want to acknowledge that being a new mother can be both incredibly rewarding and challenging. It's normal to experience a range of emotions, and I'm here to listen without judgment. The questions I'll be asking are about your feelings over the past 7 days. Let's take this one step at a time, and we'll go through the questions together.

To start, I'd like to ask: <sym>How have you been feeling lately?</sym> More specifically, <med>Have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?</med>

To be honest, I haven't been laughing much lately. I mean, I try to, but it just doesn't come as naturally as it used to. I feel like I'm just going through the motions of taking care of my baby, and that's it. I used to enjoy watching comedies or hanging out with friends who make me laugh, but now it all just feels like so much effort. Occasionally, when my baby does something cute, I might crack a smile, but it's not the same as really laughing or finding the humor in things like I used to. It feels like a part of me is just...dull. I guess that's the best way to put it.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

As I think about it, I'd say that would be "not as much as I used to." I mean, I do smile sometimes when my baby does something adorable, but it's not like I'm laughing out loud or finding humor in things like I normally would. It's like my sense of humor is just a bit muted right now.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

That's a tough one... I would say "less than usual". To be honest, I've been feeling a bit disconnected from the things I used to enjoy. I mean, I love my baby, of course, but aside from that, I don't really feel like doing much of anything else. I used to love reading, or going for walks, or just spending time with friends, but now it all feels like a chore. I don't really look forward to anything, except maybe getting a few minutes of sleep, but even that's not always possible. It feels like I'm just going through the motions, you know.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

.. I think I'd say "yes, some of the time". I feel like I'm constantly worried that I'm not doing enough for my baby, or that I'm doing something wrong. Even when things are really beyond my control, I still feel like it's my fault. Like, if my baby cries a lot, I feel like I'm not doing something right, or that I'm not a good enough mother. It's like this guilt is always lurking in the back of my mind, and it's hard to shake. It's not always there, but it's often enough that it's starting to get to me.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

.. I'd say "yes, quite a lot". I'm always on edge, worrying about my baby's health and safety. I know it's normal to worry as a new mom, but it feels like it's more than that. I worry about things like SIDS, or accidents, or just that I'm not doing enough to keep my baby safe. Sometimes I'll be sitting there, holding my baby, and I'll just start to feel this wave of anxiety wash over me, and I don't know why. It's like my mind is just racing with all these worst-case scenarios. It's hard to calm down, even when I know everything is okay.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

.. I'd say "yes, sometimes". It's similar to the anxiety I was just talking about, but it's more intense. Sometimes I'll be alone with my baby, and I'll just start to feel this overwhelming sense of fear. I don't know what's causing it, it just feels like something is wrong, or that I'm not capable of taking care of my baby. It's like my heart is racing, and I feel like I'm going to...I don't know, freak out or something. It's hard to explain. It's not all the time, but when it does happen, it's really scary.
Things have been getting on top of me

.. I'd say "yes, most of the time". To be honest, it feels like everything is just piling up on me. Caring for my baby is a lot of work, and I'm just so tired all the time. I feel like I'm not doing anything else, just taking care of my baby and trying to keep my head above water. Sometimes I feel like I'm just barely holding it together, and that if one more thing goes wrong, I'll just...collapse, I guess. It's hard to explain, but it feels like I'm just on the verge of being overwhelmed all the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

.. I'd say "yes, most of the time". I've been having a really hard time sleeping, and it's not just because of the baby waking up at night. Even when my baby is sleeping, I find it hard to fall asleep or stay asleep because I'm just lying there feeling really down and overwhelmed. I feel like my mind is racing, and I just can't seem to shut it off. I'll be lying there thinking about all the things I need to do, or worrying about my baby, or just feeling really sad and hopeless. It's like my brain just won't turn off, and it's hard to get the rest I need.
I have felt sad or miserable

.. I'd say "yes, quite often". I feel like I'm just really down a lot of the time. It's not all the time, but often enough that it's starting to feel normal. I'll be doing something, like feeding my baby or changing a diaper, and suddenly I'll just feel this wave of sadness wash over me. It's hard to explain, but it feels like I'm just really disconnected from...everything, I guess. I feel like I'm just going through the motions, and that I'm not really feeling anything deeply. Sometimes I'll start crying, and I don't even know why. It's just...it's a really hard feeling to describe.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

.. I'd say "yes, quite often". I've been crying a lot lately, usually when I'm feeling really overwhelmed or sad. It's not all the time, but a few times a week, definitely. Sometimes it's just a few tears, and sometimes I'll cry for a while. It's usually when I'm alone, or when I'm feeling like I'm just not doing enough for my baby. It's hard to explain, but it feels like all these emotions are just building up inside me, and sometimes they just spill out. It's a relief, in a way, but it's also really scary because I don't know what's going to trigger it next.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

No, not at all. I mean, I've had some really tough days and I've felt overwhelmed, but I've never thought about harming myself. I just want to be a good mom and take care of my baby, and I love them more than anything. I just feel like I'm struggling right now, but I'm not thinking about hurting myself or anything like that.

This new mother is experiencing a range of challenging emotions and symptoms consistent with potential <med>postpartum depression</med> and <med>anxiety</med>. She reports feeling overwhelmed, sad, and disconnected from activities she once enjoyed. Her EPDS responses indicate significant distress, including <sym>reduced ability to laugh</sym>, <sym>decreased enjoyment in activities</sym>, <sym>unnecessary self-blame</sym>, <sym>anxiety</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbances</sym>. Despite these challenges, she denies any thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 21, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>The patient indicates their sense of humor is 'muted' and they don't laugh out loud like they used to, aligning with 'Definitely not so much now'.</sym>, <sym>The patient states they've been feeling disconnected from things they used to enjoy and mentions looking forward to things 'less than usual', aligning with 'Definitely less than I used to</sym>, <sym>The patient states 'yes, some of the time' and elaborates on feelings of guilt and self-blame when things go wrong, matching the 'Yes, some of the time' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient describes being 'always on edge' and experiencing frequent waves of anxiety, indicating a high frequency of anxiety.</sym>, <sym>The patient explicitly states 'yes, sometimes', matching the corresponding EPDS guideline option.</sym>, <sym>Patient's response indicates feeling overwhelmed 'most of the time' and struggling to cope, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all'.</sym>, <sym>The patient explicitly states 'yes, most of the time' and elaborates on having difficulty sleeping due to feeling down, overwhelmed, and having a racing mind, matching the 'Yes, most of the time' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient states 'yes, quite often' and describes frequent feelings of sadness and disconnection, matching the 'Yes, quite often' option.</sym>, <sym>The patient states 'yes, quite often' and elaborates on crying a few times a week when feeling overwhelmed or sad, matching the 'Yes, quite often' guideline.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** The patient's EPDS score of 21 indicates a high risk for <med>postpartum depression</med>. Her responses align with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>, including <sym>depressed mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest in activities</sym>, <sym>feelings of worthlessness</sym>, and <sym>sleep disturbances</sym>. The presence of <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym> further complicates her clinical picture. While she denies <sym>suicidal ideation</sym>, the severity of her symptoms warrants urgent attention. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>PCP</med> or <med>mental health specialist</med>
2. Encourage sleep hygiene practices
3. Offer emotional support and validate her experiences
4. Consider <med>counseling</med> or <med>therapy</med> to address <sym>depression</sym> and <sym>anxiety</sym>
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 21: **Postpartum Depression Screening Summary**

**Main Symptoms and Concerns:**

* Reduced ability to laugh and enjoy things (Q1)
* Decreased enjoyment in activities (Q2)
* Unnecessary self-blame and guilt (Q3)
* Anxiety and worry for no good reason (Q4)
* Feelings of fear and panic (Q5)
* Feeling overwhelmed and struggling to cope (Q6)
* Difficulty sleeping due to emotional distress (Q7)
* Frequent feelings of sadness and misery (Q8)
* Crying spells (Q9)

**Patterns and Areas of Concern:**

* Consistent reports of low mood, loss of enjoyment, and anxiety
* Feelings of guilt, worthlessness, and self-blame
* Difficulty coping with stress and emotions
* Sleep disturbances linked to emotional distress

**Screening Significance:**

* Symptoms are consistent with potential postpartum depression and anxiety
* Reports of persistent sadness, loss of pleasure, and crying spells are concerning
* Feelings of guilt, anxiety, and being overwhelmed are significant

**Risk Factors:**

* Persistent sadness and loss of pleasure
* Sleep difficulties linked to mood
* Feelings of worthlessness or guilt
* Anxiety, panic, or being overwhelmed

**Safety Concerns:**

* No indication of self-harm or suicidal thoughts (Q10)

**Screening Observation Summary:**

The patient reports a range of symptoms consistent with potential postpartum depression and anxiety, including low mood, loss of enjoyment, anxiety, guilt, and difficulty coping. While there are no indications of self-harm or suicidal thoughts, the patient's symptoms suggest a need for further evaluation and potential support. The patient's emotional distress and sleep disturbances are significant concerns that warrant clinical attention.
